items.title: The sell-off for tech stocks deepens and drags Wall Street toward its worst day since June
items.description: A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high.

items._ogDesc: A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high.
items.body:
NEW YORK — A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high.

The S&P 500 dropped 1.8 per cent and was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the month. The Nasdaq composite was likewise heading toward its worst day since June, as the weakness for technology stocks dragged it down three per cent, as of 12:55 p.m. Eastern time. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 496 points, or 0.9 per cent.

Intel’s stock led the way downward and is flirting with its worst day since 1974 after tumbling 30.1 per cent. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Amazon sank 2.3 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through US$42.4 billion of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record and almost single-handedly dragged the S&P 500 lower after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI.

Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centers have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.

“We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors.

A drop of 4.7 per cent for the stock price of Nvidia, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, even more than Intel.

In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion worth of crypto at Binance.

Coinbase Global fell 12.9 per cent even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about four per cent of the total supply of bitcoin, fell six per cent. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons.

Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose in the S&P 500 index as fell.

ExxonMobil climbed 1.8 per cent, and Chevron added 1.6 per cent after the oil giants both reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected.

Mondelez International rose 3.7 per cent after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth.

Colgate-Palmolive climbed 3.5 per cent after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected.

Expectations are high for U.S. companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.

In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Thursday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month.

Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields higher because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4 per cent to $113.50. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher.

In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Europe following sharper swings in Asia.

South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5 per cent as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5 per cent.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1 per cent after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank.

AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

items._ogDesc: Top Picks from Brianne Gardner, Senior Wealth Manager, Velocity Investment Partners, Raymond James
items.body:
Brianne Gardner, Senior Wealth Manager, Velocity Investment Partners, Raymond James

Focus: Canadian & U.S. Large Caps

Top Picks: Home Depot, JPMorgan Chase, ASML

It’s been an interesting few weeks for investors. We’ve seen some of the biggest technology companies disappoint on earnings, while others reported strong results only to watch their shares fall. And I think that tells us something important about where the market is heading.

For the first few years, investors were willing to pay a premium for companies benefiting from artificial intelligence. There were some occasional discussions about whether the heavy investment into artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure would translate into profits, and over the last few months that conversation has gotten louder. With expectations already so high, companies have very little room for disappointment.

The good news is that the broader economy continues to hold up well. The U.S. economy grew 3.4 per cent last quarter, consumers are still spending, and corporate earnings remain healthy. Profit taking from one sector is not leaving the market, it’s rotating into other sectors. So we see an opportunity for market leadership to broaden beyond technology into healthcare, utilities, industrials and financials.

In Canada, the picture is different. Economic growth has been more challenging, with trade uncertainty and now even higher interest rates putting pressure on households and businesses. But Canada has something the world increasingly needs: energy, critical minerals and reliable natural resources. That’s why we continue to favour quality energy producers, precious metals and selected financial companies.

Of course, inflation and interest rates remain risks, so we’re balancing our technology exposure with quality businesses across sectors and international markets.

Ultimately, we believe markets will continue to advance, but earnings, valuations and diversification will matter much more going forward.

  • Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters

Home Depot (HD NYSE)

We like Home Depot as a new pick because we believe it is well positioned to benefit when the U.S. housing market eventually recovers.

Home Depot is much more than a home improvement retailer. It serves homeowners and professional contractors, selling everything needed to renovate, repair and maintain homes. The housing market has been holding it back. High mortgage rates mean fewer people are moving, while homeowners are postponing expensive renovations like kitchens and bathrooms. The latest quarter showed some improvement.

Sales grew nearly six per cent, and Home Depot continued gaining market share, even though customers are still making fewer trips to its stores. The big opportunity is a housing recovery. As mortgage rates ease and people start moving again, demand for renovations should return, helping Home Depot grow earnings.

We like Home Depot as a way to position for that recovery. Demand remains soft and valuation isn’t particularly cheap, but its strong market position makes it an attractive long-term opportunity.

JPMorgan Chase (JPM NYSE)

We own JPMorgan Chase and continue to like it as one of the strongest banks in the United States, with several ways to grow even in an uncertain economy.

JPMorgan is much more than a traditional bank. It serves everyday customers, manages investments and helps some of the world’s largest companies raise money and expand. The latest quarter was a little disappointing. Earnings missed expectations, partly because the bank set aside more money for potential loan losses, even though customers continue paying their debts. The underlying business remains strong.

Investment banking fees grew 14 per cent, while trading activity and demand for loans remained healthy, showing businesses are still active. The outlook is actually improving. JPMorgan expects to earn more from lending next year than previously anticipated, supported by healthy loan growth and interest rates.

We continue to like JPMorgan. Rising expenses and economic uncertainty are worth watching, but its diversified business and strong financial position make it a core banking holding.

We own ASML and continue to like it as one of the most important companies behind the AI revolution. ASML makes the machines that make the chips. Its technology is essential for producing the advanced semiconductors powering AI, and it has virtually no competition. Latest results were strong. Earnings beat expectations, orders remained healthy, and customers continued upgrading their machines.

AI demand is growing so quickly that ASML is looking to expand production capacity further, creating opportunities for future growth. The stock pulled back despite good results. Investors worried about AI spending and whether expansion costs could put pressure on profit margins.

We remain confident in the long-term story. Valuation is a consideration, but ASML’s unique technology and growing demand make it one of our favourite semiconductor holdings.

items.title: Houston resists calls for legislation as AI data centre backlash grows
items.description: Julissa Stewart says she panicked when she learned about plans for an 18,600-square-metre AI data centre at an industrial site about 20 minutes away from her home in southern Cape Breton.

items._ogDesc: Julissa Stewart says she panicked when she learned about plans for an 18,600-square-metre AI data centre at an industrial site about 20 minutes away from her home in southern Cape Breton.
items.body:
HALIFAX — Julissa Stewart says she panicked when she learned about plans for an 18,600-square-metre AI data centre at an industrial site about 20 minutes away from her home in southern Cape Breton.

Earlier this month, EverWind Fuels announced it intends to set up a $10-billion AI data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., that would come online by the end of 2027.

The American AI company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for the centre, which would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase. The company says a 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028, which would bring the development’s total energy demand to 420 megawatts.

“I’ve been paying attention to what’s happening with AI data centres in other places in Canada and in the States … then hearing that it’s coming here, so close to where we live, I have serious concerns. Not because I’m against economic development, but because of how this is being rolled out,” Stewart said in a recent interview.

The project by EverWind and Anthropic has thrust Nova Scotia into a debate that is playing out across Canada and the United States, as technology companies scramble to find locations for data centres needed to deliver the power for artificial intelligence and other computing infrastructure.

In many cases, it has placed politicians eager for major industrial investments at odds with neighbourhoods filled with suspicion and anxiety about what’s planned in their backyards.

Stewart said she’s been shocked by the speed of EverWind’s plan and lack of consultation with the community.

EverWind’s chief financial officer said Tuesday the company was unable to start community consultation ahead of the Oct. 16 announcement because of a strict non-disclosure agreement with Anthropic. Information sessions hosted by EverWind are scheduled to begin in the Richmond County area next week.

Stewart, who plans to attend, is also skeptical about how Premier Tim Houston appears to have shifted his views about data centres over the past few months.

“The way this has been rolling out has been very upsetting to people,” Stewart said.

On June 18, Houston said it was too soon to turn his government’s attention to the matter, and a discussion about data centres would happen “far out into the future.”

By late September, he softened that stance, opening a door to consider proposals from the sector in a post on social media.

“Then all of a sudden, we’re finding out this is coming to our backyard,” Stewart said.

She said her biggest concern is the lack of environmental assessment for the project and a shortage of regulations. Houston told reporters Wednesday it’s not clear to him if any new legislation is needed.

“Do we want to do a piece of legislation for every business that sets up in Nova Scotia? Probably not. I mean, we’ve got to be realistic about these things. We have guidelines. We have approval processes. And they’ll be followed,” the premier said.

Lora MacEachern, deputy minister of environment and climate change, said Tuesday the data centre doesn’t need to go through an environmental assessment and the industrial approval process is sufficient.

AI data centres are not on the list of projects that would automatically trigger an environmental assessment in Nova Scotia. This list includes quarries, mines, energy generation projects and other industrial facilities.

The premier suggested AI data centres do not need to be on the list.

“We have guidelines that have to be met around water usage … around power rates. The government shouldn’t care what type of company it is, the government should care that the requirements of the province are met, and we’ll make sure that’s the case,” he said.

Stewart said legally binding regulations could help reassure residents about EverWind’s promise to behave responsibly.

“We can’t just rely on a company’s word. It’s not good enough,” Stewart said. “What if this project gets built and it’s not what was advertised?”

Less than two weeks after EverWind’s announcement, a petition to stop the development of AI data centres in Nova Scotia on Change.org garnered more than 24,000 signatures.

Opposition parties have also called for legislated regulations for AI data centres and for an environmental assessment to be conducted.

NDP Leader Claudia Chender said legally binding regulations are essential given the “long history of large industrial projects in Nova Scotia leaving us with … decades of pollution, huge environmental implications, huge social implications.”

EverWind’s chief financial officer, Matthew Tinari, told a Nova Scotia legislature committee Tuesday that residents deserve clear and factual answers to their questions and the company is committed to addressing concerns.

Tinari said this includes a commitment to prevent rate hikes for residential electricity customers as well as a promise to protect the water supply and minimize water use. He also said the project would follow federal and provincial guidelines for data centres.

“What we’ve heard from community is (that) industry should have binding commitments. So we were proposing to the province some type of agreement like that,” Tinari said.

Houston would not say if his Progressive Conservative government would require a legally binding agreement.

Vaibhav Bahadur, a professor in mechanical engineering at the University of Texas at Austin, specializes in AI data centres in a state that has welcomed massive data centre development. He said “industries don’t like regulations, but in my opinion, you do need to balance what industry wants with environmental concerns and obviously concerns from the general public.”

The University of Texas maintains a database of all data centres in the state. Bahadur says there are about 300 of them running and another 300 or so in various stages of planning or development.

While America is home to far larger data centres than the one EverWind is proposing in Cape Breton, Bahadur said the 95-megawatt facility is significant.

“There’s bound to be concerns when you’re talking about that amount of power going into one facility,” he said in a recent interview.

EverWind says it will cover the cost of all electricity infrastructure, which is why the project will not increase power rates for customers.

The company also says the project will include a closed-loop cooling system using recycled water as well as an external cooling system that would require the use of additional water on very hot days.

On average, EverWind estimates the system would use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day from the nearby Landrie Lake in the first phase and an average of 500,000 litres per day when the expansion is complete. Tinari said the peak demand represents 1.5 per cent of the lake’s estimated sustainable daily yield.

Bahadur said based on the location of the planned data centre in Point Tupper, he expects it would use far less water compared to AI data centres in hotter climates, such as Texas.

Paris Marx, a Newfoundland and Labrador-based tech critic and author of “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” says AI companies have learned from the opposition they’ve encountered in the United States over the past couple of years and are trying to head off environmental criticism before it starts.

He said companies are aware of concerns around water use, which is why they’re pivoting from evaporative cooling systems and constant water use in favour of closed-loop systems.

Marx said those closed-loop systems have only seriously been contemplated over the last six to eight months.

“Right now it sounds good because it’s just like, `Oh, we’re using less water,”' Marx said in a recent interview.

“But the companies aren’t coming out and being completely transparent about what the trade-offs of that are.”

He said the trade-offs could include the need for using substances such as coolants and the need for more energy to keep the system running.

Bahadur said closed-loop cooling systems have been around for a few years in the United States, and they are a more recent development in Canada. He also agreed that closed-loop systems require more electricity than other cooling options and that there could be broader concerns about pollution, which are not limited to data centres.

The electricity required for a closed-loop system will result in additional water use in Nova Scotia, Bahadur said, because the province still relies on fossil fuels like coal to produce electricity.

“My overall opinion is that under cold climate conditions like in Nova Scotia, water use shouldn’t be much of a concern, especially if the data centre is using state-of-art technologies, and being responsible -- which can require regulations in place,” Bahadur said in an email.

Stewart said she’s worried about what may happen to Richmond County’s environment and water supply if the project is not held to high environmental standards that extend into the future.

“I have a six-year-old daughter, and I have concerns about this down the road. If we don’t put proper regulations in place, what is that going to look like for her? … What are the health risks? We don’t have enough information,” she said.

A recent United Nations University report says the environmental footprint of data centres globally already rivals some of the world’s largest countries. The report also predicts their water and energy use and pollution will double in just four years as use of artificial intelligence grows.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

— With files from Devin Stevens

Lyndsay Armstrong, The Canadian Press

items.title: Timing of next rate hike in question after surprise stall in August GDP
items.description: Signs that economic growth stalled over the summer have some economists debating the timing of the Bank of Canada’s next interest rate hike.
items._ogDesc: Signs that economic growth stalled over the summer have some economists debating the timing of the Bank of Canada’s next interest rate hike.
items.body:
Signs that economic growth stalled over the summer have some economists debating the timing of the Bank of Canada’s next interest rate hike.

Statistics Canada said Friday that real gross domestic product was essentially unchanged for a second straight month in August. That fell short of economists’ calls and the agency’s own early expectations for a gain of 0.2 per cent in the month.

Wholesale trade fell 1.4 per cent in August as most subsectors contracted. StatCan said motor vehicle and vehicle parts wholesalers faced their first decline in seven months amid lower vehicle imports and weaker manufacturing activity in the subsector.

StatCan cited a “prolonged summer shutdown at a major auto assembly plant” to explain a 5.8 per cent decline in motor vehicles and parts manufacturing in August.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Tu Nguyen, chief economist at RSM Canada, said what’s notable about the August declines in these sectors is they would only partially capture the impacts of a breakdown in trade talks between Canada and the United States that month.

Both sides have since levied new waves of tariffs and trade restrictions against one another.

Manufacturing and wholesale trade — sectors that are particularly vulnerable to tariff disruptions — will continue to see regular contractions under the re-escalated trade dispute, Nguyen said.

Elsewhere, StatCan said work to prepare the 2026 census was still winding down in August, driving widespread contractions in public administration.

Maintenance work at some nuclear power plants and mining facilities in northern Alberta also dragged on growth that month, StatCan said.

Retail trade, manufacturing as a whole and the transportation and warehousing industries were among those posting gains to offset the declines in August.

StatCan’s early estimates for September suggest real GDP declined 0.1 per cent, driven by losses in manufacturing and mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction.

The agency’s flash estimates still see real GDP expanding 1.3 per cent on an annualized basis in the third quarter, a slowdown from 3.3 per cent growth in the second quarter.

StatCan will provide its official quarterly estimates for the third quarter next month when it reports the September GDP figures.

BMO chief economist Doug Porter said in a note to clients Friday that some of the weakness last quarter might be overstated, particularly as it relates to census-related slowdowns.

“Still, with the trade tiff still flaring, housing struggling, and recent employment figures concerning, it certainly appears that growth has run into some pretty serious headwinds of late,” he said.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

The latest economic data comes two days after the Bank of Canada raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent, the first hike in more than three years.

An increase to the central bank’s key rate will typically take some steam out of the economy, though most analysts still see current monetary policy levels as somewhat stimulative.

Officials at the central bank argued this week that a rate hike was warranted to get ahead of looming inflation risks. Governor Tiff Macklem pointed to signs of resilience in the Canadian economy over the spring in justifying the decision.

The central bank also revised up its expectations for growth on Wednesday. Monetary policymakers are expecting growth in the third quarter ended up at two per cent on an annualized basis, up from 1.5 per cent in its July forecasts.

Many economists weighing in Friday argued the Bank of Canada’s somewhat rosier projections are at risk after StatCan data suggested middling growth in the third quarter.

BMO, which had been in line with the central bank’s call for two per cent growth, trimmed its outlook to 1.5 per cent after Friday’s surprise.

The Bank of Canada is expecting a further slowdown in the fourth quarter will give way to real GDP growth of two per cent in 2027 and 2028.

Nguyen said despite the recent stumbles, there are reasons for optimism in the year ahead. Government spending priorities for a build out of major projects and tax incentives for business investment should give the economy a lift in 2027, she argued.

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC, said in a note that the August data suggested the economy “was already struggling for momentum even before this week’s interest rate hike.”

A slower-than-expected economy could help relieve inflationary pressures and reduce the need for additional rate hikes, he added.

The weak GDP results support a pause from the Bank of Canada at its final rate decision of the year in December, Grantham said, though he noted there’s plenty of additional economic data to come before that meeting.

Financial market odds of an interest rate hike on Dec. 9 stood at 57 per cent as of Friday morning, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.

Nguyen said it’s a “coin flip” whether the Bank of Canada hikes in December or its next meeting in January. But given Macklem’s comments this week focused on economic resilience and inflationary fears, she said she leans toward a second quarter-point hike sooner than later.

“A 25-basis-point hike, one month apart, whether in December or in January, I don’t think would change too much in terms of growth trajectory,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

items.body:
MONTREAL -- Prime Minister Mark Carney and his European Union counterparts are closing a major summit by announcing what they call an alliance for the future.

A joint statement calls for more industrial collaboration and supply chain integration and cites various current joint projects.

This is a breaking news update. More information to come.

Original article from The Canadian Press follows.

MONTREAL -- A major summit Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting with European Union leaders is set to conclude Friday with announcements on digital trade and academic exchanges.

Carney welcomed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa to the Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Thursday.

Carney, Von der Leyen and Costa all said Thursday they would like to see Canada become an “associate member” of the European Union, despite countries like Germany rejecting that term and Canadian officials initially avoiding that phrasing.

None of the leaders used the term “associate member” during welcoming remarks to the gathering on Friday. Instead, they said the goal is to bring Canada closer to the EU than any other non-European nation.

While these meetings have been happening for years, this one sees Canada and the EU scaling up their efforts to deepen their commercial and diplomatic relationship.

Costa said he expects to see an agreement on digital trade finalized Friday, and news on programs for scientific research partnerships and university student exchanges.

Costa added Thursday he wants to see greater labour mobility between Canada and Europe and easier student exchanges.

Culture Minister Marc Miller said Thursday any discussions of labour mobility in industries like film production would need to include the provinces, many of which have their own tax credits that promote local talent.

Miller has been meeting with his European counterparts at the summit. He has been talking about setting new regulations on promoting Canadian and European content on streaming services, along with new safeguards for children online.

“So two issues that are really important, and we’re not talking about the same exact rules potentially, but convergence and allyship with respect to large transnational companies that in some cases need to be regulated to protect kids or to promote our cultures in the face of overwhelming, monopolistic cultures, one of which is the United States, but others across the world,” Miller said in an interview.

Miller said officials are also looking at ways to increase the number of co-productions between Canada and Europe like the TV series Vikings, a Canadian-Irish co-production.

The minister said Canada already has co-production treaties with several European countries that allow pooling of tax credits to attract film and TV show productions.

Miller said he brought his EU counterparts to one of the promotional events for the documentary Villeneuve: The Rise of a Legend, about Quebec Formula One driver Gilles Villeneuve, which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival. He said part of the goal was to secure a theatrical release for the film in Europe.

Conservatives have criticized the summit, noting that nine of the 28 countries in the EU have yet to ratify a decade-old trade deal with Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

items.body:
MONTREAL — Canadian National Railway Co. saw profits perk up last quarter as the country’s largest railroad operator rode a surge in grain and fuel shipments amid Canada’s more “positive” investment milieu, its CEO says.

The Montreal-based company on Friday reported a six per cent year-over-year jump in third-quarter net income to $1.21 billion.

Revenues rose 14.5 per cent to $4.77 billion, though some of the extra cash went to cover fuel costs, which leaped 56 per cent from the same period a year earlier.

“Energy continues to be a key growth driver,” said chief executive Tracy Robinson on a call with analysts.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Petroleum and chemical hauls brought in precisely $1 billion in revenue, 17 per cent more than last year.

The tail end of a bumper grain crop also propelled a similar percentage increase in that category.

While CN made no changes to its 2026 financial forecast, Robinson was upbeat about longer-term growth prospects under what she framed as Prime Minister Mark Carney’s more business-friendly government, and despite persistent tariff troubles that have hampered some sectors.

“The Carney administration has leaned into creating a more positive environment for investment,” she said, citing regulatory and tax changes, such as a provision that allows businesses to write off 100 per cent of some new investments.

“This is a very constructive environment and it’s focused on getting Canada’s natural resources, which are in high demand, to markets across the continent and around the world.”

Robinson also noted that a “soon-to-be-finalized” deal with Union Pacific will give Canadian National access to the Mexican manufacturing corridor, as it will grant CN the right to run trains over UP tracks between Memphis and Eagle Pass, TX, which sits along the Rio Grande.

Centering on cars, manufacturing and food, trade between Canada and Mexico amounts to some US$45 billion dollars each year, “much of which is tied to Eastern Canada,” where CN has a more extensive network than rival Canadian Pacific Kanas City Ltd., she said. On the other hand, CPKC boasts the only rail network to span all three countries in North America, handing it even more fluid access to the Mexican market.

On the tariff front, trade along CN tracks has stabilized for now, with some auto, steel and forest shipments rerouted beyond the United States, executives said.

“There are some sectors that are disproportionately and uniquely impacted ... and there are some adjustments that have been made there around the kinds of markets that they’re shipping into,” Robinson said.

“We’ve overcome the $350 million of tariff headwinds from last year,” added chief commercial officer Janet Drysdale.

Domestically, CN faced an emergency in July when a crew had to be evacuated from a train engulfed in flames in northwestern Ontario.

A video of the incident shared widely on social media showed a curtain of orange-red flames closing in on the train near Armstrong, Ont., as trees burned on both sides of the tracks.

Two other crews were also evacuated from trains stopped in their tracks by the blazes.

CN temporarily suspended rail operations in a portion of northwestern Ontario on July 13, halting all freight traffic along a stretch of main-line track crucial to cross-country hauls.

Federal authorities are looking into whether the company broke the law.

On Friday, CN said it earned $2.16 per adjusted diluted share in its latest quarter, up from an adjusted profit of $1.83 per diluted share a year ago and beating analysts’ expectations of $2.10 per share, according to financial markets firm LSEG Data & Analytics.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

By Christopher Reynolds

items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Eric Ham says Trump’s aggressive trade offensive is backfiring domestically, uniting U.S. citizens, businesses, and Republican lawmakers in defense of Canada’s sovereignty (Getty Images / Wong Yu Liang)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: From tariff powers to trade leverage, Washington political analyst Eric Ham breaks down everything Canadians need to know ahead of next week’s crucial U.S. midterm elections.
items.body:
Eric Ham is based in Washington, D.C. and is a political analyst for CTV News. He’s a bestselling author and former congressional staffer and writes for CTVNews.ca.

From tariff powers to trade leverage, Ham breaks down what Canadians need to know ahead of next week’s crucial U.S. midterm elections.

What impact, if any, will the U.S. midterms have on talks between Ottawa and Washington?

It is unclear how earnest actual negotiations are as voters gear up to head to the polls. Still, Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump are attempting to drive a narrative in the closing days of tightly contested races that will shape the balance of power in Washington and ultimately relations between the two neighbours.

Talks failed back in August as the prime minister ended negotiations. The White House imposed tariffs on a bevy of goods in response, with Ottawa retaliating. Since that time each country has implemented import duties on billions of goods.

President Trump announced Liberation Day tariffs more than a year ago, so why is the White House moving on tariffs now?

According to a poll conducted by the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank headquartered in Washington, D.C., 75% of all registered voters surveyed said that tariffs will be “important” for their vote in this year’s midterms. Moreover, a Fox News poll conducted in September found that 64% of respondents said tariffs hurt the U.S. economy. A Marquette Poll found that 70% of those surveyed disapprove of Trump’s handling of tariffs.

Nevertheless, the White House has continued to double down on this ruinous economic policy even as the American people reject the import taxes. Now as the president finds his administration universally loathed as a result, it appears to be costing his party in an off-year election. Even traditional red states Trump won in just 2024 by double-digits are now in play for Democrats. Historically conservative Kansas, home to 1,500 jobs directly tied to Canadian defence contractor Bombardier, was being targeted by the White House in its ongoing trade war with Canada.

Yet, as polls showed races in the state tightening and Democrats with a real shot at winning a statewide office for the first time since 1931, the administration has abruptly changed course recently, rescinding tariffs.

Who holds leverage in current trade talks?

President Trump, speaking to reporters at the White House just last week, stated it was the United States that “holds all the cards.” However, just this week, the prime minister said the Trump administration is “coming closer to our position.

Carney made the comments during a question-and-answer period with reporters after a meeting between First Nation leaders and First Ministers in Ottawa on Monday. Yet, as voters head to the polls—seemingly ready to oust Trump’s party from power—it is clear that all leverage, at least for now, rests with Ottawa.

If Democrats succeed in winning back control of Congress, what does that mean for the ongoing trade war and the president’s tariffs?

Democrats have vowed to rescind all of the Trump tariffs as well as trade authorities within the first 100 hours of taking office. A tall order indeed that will require a veto-proof majority of Congress to pass the legislation necessary to undo the tariffs enacted by the White House.

As for the actual trade authorities themselves exercised by the Trump administration, that, too, could be undone by Congress, provided the votes exist. The Constitution gives primary commercial and tariff authority to Congress, the executive branch’s current influence over trade does not come directly from the text of the Constitution. Instead, it comes from statutes passed by Congress over decades (especially since the Second World War and the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934) that delegate specific authorities to the president.

Those authorities include:

  • Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act;
  • Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974;
  • International Emergency Economic Powers Act; and the
  • Trade Promotion Authority (TPA) All of these have been used by this White House to increase prices on goods coming across the border.

A new Congress can author legislation to override existing laws that will dramatically curtail the Executive Branch’s trade powers. Success, of course, depends on enough Democrats winning next week to outright pass bills to withstand a White House veto.

How many votes are needed to override a presidential veto?

Congress needs a two-thirds majority vote in both chambers. The specific number is based on the total number of members present for an actual vote. Should Democrats succeed in winning back both chambers, there is still no guarantee they will succeed in rescinding Trump’s tariffs on Canada. Congressman Hakeem Jeffries would likely make history as the first person of colour to ascend to the position of Speaker of the House.

  • More opinions and expert analyses

In such a powerful role he is untested and it is unclear if he has the political influence to rally his caucus to take very difficult votes that would directly usurp the muscular authority of perhaps the most powerful chief executive since Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Moreover, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has largely underwhelmed and nothing in his tenure suggests a willingness to engage in political pugilism with a Trump-led White House.

What happens if Democrats do not secure victory in both chambers of Congress? Will they still be able to rescind presidential trade authorities and tariffs?

Even with the votes to challenge the president, it is going to be a monumental challenge. Yet, without control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats simply do not have the votes to override a presidential veto as they would need Republican support.

President Trump, as a lame-duck president, still controls congressional Republicans with an iron fist. Democrats might be able to stifle, delay, and thwart the White House legislative agenda, but undoing presidential trade authority is practically impossible without the votes to override a veto. Moreover, because the president has largely bypassed Congress, relying on executive orders to swiftly enact his agenda, delay tactics, too, would prove fruitless without absolute control of both chambers.

items.title: Gone in 20 minutes: How the biggest heist in crypto history unfolded
items.description: Hackers stole US$6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record digital asset theft.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Binance logo is seen on a smartphone, Feb. 28, 2023, in Marple Township, Pa. (AP Photo/Matt Slocum, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Matt Slocum</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Hackers stole US$6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record digital asset theft.
items.body:
SINGAPORE -- Hackers stole US$6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record digital asset theft.

Here’s what we know so far:

What happened?

About $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies were drained from wallets that Binance uses to process transactions, according to the exchange and expert analysis of blockchain records.

Binance said in a statement on X that it initially thought the attack involved a compromised laptop. “However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” it added, without elaborating.

The exchange operates a secure asset fund for users, a $1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customers in the event of a security breach, according to its website.

Co-CEO Richard Teng said losses would be covered by the fund and company resources.

According to U.S. blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs, the attackers compromised Binance’s “signing infrastructure,” which authorizes transactions, allowing them to issue instructions that emptied the affected wallets.

The bulk of the heist unfolded in about 20 minutes, blockchain records show, beginning shortly after 2000 GMT on Thursday.

Once the funds were moved, the attackers raced to shift them beyond the reach of Binance counterparties and stablecoin issuers, which have frozen roughly half of the stolen assets.

An unusual feature of some cryptocurrencies, including major stablecoins such as Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC, is that their issuers can freeze them remotely.

“In layman’s terms, the attacker may not have stolen the vault key, they may have hijacked the system that tells the vault to release money,” said Joshua Chu, a Hong Kong lawyer who works on crypto cases.

Who is behind it?

Several U.S. blockchain analysis firms said the attack bears similarities to previous operations attributed to North Korean hackers.

Teng said Binance’s investigation had not yet identified the attackers, while North Korea routinely denies involvement in cyberattacks and cryptocurrency thefts. North Korea’s mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

TRM said the breach shared characteristics with last year’s attack on crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korean hackers. The firm said it was highly confident the same group was behind the Binance theft.

Chainalysis said funds stolen in an attack last month on Bitget were being mixed with proceeds from the Binance breach.

Where’s the money?

About half the stolen assets were stablecoins that have since been frozen by issuers including Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture.

That doesn’t mean the coins will be returned to Binance, but it significantly limits the attackers’ ability to convert them into cash.

TRM said some of the funds had already been posted as collateral to borrow ether and estimated that about $2.4 billion worth of bitcoin and ether is beyond reach.

Because no centralized entity issues bitcoin or ether, no one can freeze those assets, said Patrick Tan, general counsel of ChainArgos, a blockchain intelligence firm in Singapore.

“The bitcoin and ether can be stopped only if the attacker sends them to a crypto-asset exchange or broker that is able and willing to freeze them, or if law enforcement obtains the private keys.”

Market participants and analysts said the attackers would likely mix the stolen coins with other assets or use lesser-known coins and exchanges to try to move the proceeds.

Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a stablecoin infrastructure company, said typically the proceeds of such hacks can only be laundered in the first few hours.

“The more time passes, the less likely they will be able to fold those funds into other exchanges or payment providers — they essentially get blacklisted.”

Chainalysis said in a post on its website that its investigators were observing laundering patterns they had not seen before. “Thousands of transactions in a short period suggest that the attackers are using automation to obscure the trail of funds. Rather than simply moving funds onward, they repeatedly circulate them among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses involved earlier in the sequence,” it wrote.

What next?

The theft is the latest in a series of major digital asset breaches. Attackers stole $2.9 billion of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to TRM Labs.

The attack has also rattled confidence in the sector. Cryptocurrencies fell on Friday and the total market value of stablecoins declined, suggesting investors were pulling money from digital assets.

By Ankur Banerjee and Rae Wee, Reuters

Additional reporting by Tom Westbrook in Singapore and Hannah Lang in New York. Editing by Michelle Price and Mark Potter

items._ogDesc: Walmart Inc. has brought its AI chatbot Sparky to Canada, more than a year after the retailer first rolled out the shopping assistant in the United States.
items.body:
MISSISSAUGA — Walmart Inc. has brought its AI chatbot Sparky to Canada, more than a year after the retailer first rolled out the shopping assistant in the United States.

The chatbot allows consumers to find and compare products or assist in building a shopping list.

Andrew Go, vice-president of e-commerce at Walmart Canada, says Sparky can help consumers with questions and plan shopping lists based on a specific budget or an occasion such as a holiday meal.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

Walmart CEO John Furner last month vowed that its AI shopping assistant will not use personal information such as income or shopping history to set personalized prices for customers or hide lower-priced options.

The pledge came as concerns grew from some shoppers skeptical about the rollout of digital price labels and the retailer’s push to integrate AI.

Meanwhile, Loblaw Cos. Ltd. integrated its grocery delivery app into OpenAI’s chatbot ChatGPT in February — a first among grocers.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

Canada and the European Union have pledged to deepen their security, digital and scholastic relationships. Leaders from both governments are in Montreal today to discuss the details, pushed by what they’ve described as a destabilized international order.

The two-day EU-Canada Summit began Thursday after months of speculation around how a new alliance between the two bodies will take shape. Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa are involved in talks – and all three have said they would like to see Canada become an “associate member” of the bloc.

Some countries, led by Germany, have bristled at that term, even as they support deepening ties across the Atlantic. Conservatives called the summit a distraction, noting that nine of the 27 countries in the EU have yet to ratify a decade-old trade deal with Canada.

items.title: The BoC isn’t expecting the housing market to heat up anytime soon
items.description: Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing
items.content: <p>Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639289754495839586.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing
items.body:
The Bank of Canada doesn’t see much chance of a hotter national housing market in the near future, forecasting this week that housing will contribute essentially nothing to national economic growth in the next two years.

The central bank said in the latest Monetary Policy Report, released alongside its rate hike on Wednesday, that climbing borrowing costs will send housing-related expenses higher in 2027 and 2028, while material and equipment prices will also increase as home construction and maintenance costs rise.

That’s not to say housing and mortgage professionals will notice a sudden or sharp change, with the deep freeze that’s gripped the market over the past two years showing no sign of thawing.

Benjamin Reitzes (pictured top), managing director, Canadian rates and macro strategist at Bank of Montreal (BMO), told Canadian Mortgage Professional the central bank’s 25-basis-point increase on October 28 may have a slight negative impact on the market, but that there wasn’t much momentum to stall in the first place.

“What’s notable is that you already had mortgage rates notably higher right across the curve. So the only point where they were contained was on the variable side,” he said. “At least half the activity was coming in variable, according to the data.

“So [the hike] will provide a bit more of a dampener, I think, on the margin. Of course it makes a difference – but it’s not as if housing was booming. And so there probably is a limit to how much weaker it gets.”

Why the housing market is still slow

The main culprits for the still-sluggish housing market are well known at this stage: economic uncertainty triggered by the US-Canada trade war, and inflation concerns as a result of surging fuel costs.

That trade dispute has sparked fears of job losses and a big hit to the economy since the beginning of last year, while rising inflation was one of the main reasons the Bank of Canada raised rates on Wednesday and could hike again soon.

And while home prices have slid across many markets in 2025 and 2026, Reitzes suggested that the correction may still have a while to run.

“The reality for the housing market is that affordability is still stretched. There’s still room for prices to fall – the affordability side of things needs to improve,” he said. “I think at this point, the path of least resistance is probably still toward modestly lower prices for housing and continued softness on that front. And that’s what the Bank’s expecting.”

Affordability improved in almost every major Canadian market in September, according to ratehub.ca, but that picture could be complicated if rates continue rising in the coming months.

Population dynamics are also playing their part in the market’s slowdown. The federal government dramatically upped its immigration targets in the early years of this decade, boosting demand for housing and rental units.

Those targets have been pared back substantially, a trend that’s lowered clamour for condo rentals in major markets – most notably Toronto – and contributed to the wider housing market cooldown.

The market’s torpor has also fuelled calls among some executives for an end or revision to the foreign homebuyer ban that’s been in place since the beginning of 2023, although industry views on the matter have been mixed.

Why a less intense housing market could ultimately benefit Canada

Reitzes emphasized that a less intense focus on the housing market could be a net positive in the long run for the Canadian economy.

“Population growth is not particularly strong in Canada at the moment, and so the dynamics are challenging for housing – and that isn’t necessarily the worst thing,” he said. “Housing has… gotten too much attention over the past few decades, and it’s kind of shifting the focus toward business investment and toward driving productivity growth in Canada.

“As much as people love to focus on housing, sometimes it’s not always the best use of capital for the country. So it’s not the end of the world here that we’re going a different way.”

items.title: Real estate lawyer talks enforcement, institutional money – and what’s next
items.description: Grechi Carter partner and founder on the current and coming trends in private and alternative lending
items.content: <p>Grechi Carter partner and founder on the current and coming trends in private and alternative lending</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639289674628824034.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Grechi Carter partner and founder on the current and coming trends in private and alternative lending
items.body:
Daniele Grechi, partner and founder at Grechi Carter Real Estate Lawyers, joins us to talk about how the private and alternative lending space has evolved, and where it’s heading. We look back at the early days of syndicate lending, loose structure and outsized returns, and how the arrival of institutional money since COVID has made private lending far more regulated and competitive.

[00:00] We're meeting a lot of people who are saying, you know, the service we used to get we're not getting anymore. The returns were just absurd for the risk levels. My general thoughts are we're close to the bottom. I think tough times make for better actions. Not every lender is doing every deal anymore.

[00:27] Fergal McAlinden: So, we are joined now by Daniele Grechi who is a partner and founder at Grechi Carter.

[00:34] Grechi Carter. Great to talk to you today. You're in an interesting space to look at how things are going in the mortgage sector and the mortgage industry as a whole. Tell us a little bit about some of the work that you're doing in the mortgage sector at the moment.

[00:46] Daniele Grechi: So, we're still quite busy with the private lending side of things. For us, the really interesting thing has been how the enforcement side of things is growing. There's obviously, with the way the market's been, a real need for that.

[01:00] I think our firm is in a very unique position because we've got a high level of expertise in that space. We've got a full team dedicated, four lawyers, three clerks. So, we can handle a high volume of work and still provide the level of service that our clients would expect.

[01:19] I know that the industry is generally kind of struggling, for lack of a better word. A lot of the big firms in this space have so much volume that we're meeting a lot of people who are saying, you know, the service we used to get we're not getting anymore. That's kind of provided a ton of opportunity for us to spread our wings and grow in this space, and we have.

[01:34] Fergal McAlinden: You mentioned you work in the private lending space. That's obviously seen a big evolution over the past few years. You mentioned that you were last year kind of pre-COVID. What have been some of the big changes that you've seen over the years in terms of how you're working with private and alternative lenders?

[01:46] Daniele Grechi: Well, it's really interesting because we've been in this space for almost 15 years now, and in the first six or seven years, it was such a different space. It was a lot of syndicate lending, a lot less structure, a lot of random different groups, small lenders, and the returns were just absurd for the risk levels that were available.

[02:05] Every year markets were going up 20%. It's sort of an easier space to operate in and because of that a ton of capital flooded to it. Since the COVID era, I think what we've seen is the flock of institutional money through the mix and they very much have professionalized the space.

[02:22] I think what we now refer to as private is kind of institutional, very regulated, very professional, extremely competitive. I think that's sort of the biggest change I've seen since we started in the business.

[02:38] Fergal McAlinden: Looking even to the next year or so, or the next few years, any kind of trends that you foresee? Do you see the space continuing to grow? Are there challenges ahead? What's in store?

[02:47] Daniele Grechi: I definitely think the space is going to grow. I think right now a lot of firms are probably going through some pain because of the change in the market, but a lot of people have adapted.

[02:58] My general thoughts are we're close to the bottom. So, hopefully things are going to move up from here. It's really forced people to have tighter processes. I think tough times make for better actions and people have had to tighten their processes, really look at their underwriting.

[03:14] And I think moving forward I see a more stable space. Opportunities are always going to be there. It's such a big market. I'm just really hoping to see the rebound in the real estate market and that everybody can get busier again.

[03:28] Fergal McAlinden: I think we're all looking ahead to that. Is there anything, Daniele, that you're speaking mostly with brokers about today or any kind of big conversations that you're hoping to have with them?

[03:36] Daniele Grechi: I mean it's always the same types of conversations. They're looking for speed, turnaround, can you handle complicated things? Is there anything different right now than we've seen in the past? No, I don't think there's anything different.

[03:48] Like I said, I think it's that theme of the people who are still working are working hard. It's tougher times, so it's forced people to become better at what they do. And that's kind of the theme right now in the real estate market.

[04:00] Fergal McAlinden: How about the event today? What's your general impressions of how it's gone?

[04:03] Daniele Grechi: A lot of energy. I've noticed a lot of people who are really, really hungry to meet as many people and learn as much as they can.

[04:12] I think it's probably tied into that, you know, not every lender is doing every deal anymore. So, you've got to go to different lenders for different needs. You've got to know your sweet spots for whatever it is that your clients need.

[04:23] So, I do really get the sense that people are here to meet different people, learn about what they do, and see how they can help them with their practice.

[04:30] Fergal McAlinden: Face-to-face conversations, it can't be overstated how important they are.

[04:34] Daniele Grechi: 100%.

[04:35] Fergal McAlinden: All right. Well, good luck with the rest of the event. Great to see you today, Daniele, and we'll talk to you soon.

[04:39] Daniele Grechi: Thanks. Great to meet you.

items.title: Ontario Municipalities Begin Slashing Development Charges As Part Of Federal Deal
items.description:
After reaching an $8.8 billion agreement on March 30 to cut development charges, the Governments of Canada and Ontario have been busy finalizing agreements with local governments to implement the changes.

The initiative is officially known as the Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) and applications opened on June 1, as previously reported by STOREYS.

The program “will deliver federal and provincial funding over 10 years for housing-enabling infrastructure projects, with funding prioritized for municipalities that reduce development charges for all residential types by 30 per cent to 50 per cent or greater and maintain the reductions for at least three years.”

Municipalities levy development charges on new construction to fund infrastructure, and this program will see the federal and provincial government fund that infrastructure, allowing municipalities to lower the levies.

The first announcements were made in late-August, with Hamilton receiving $572 million and Vaughan receiving $697.2 million.

Hamilton has committed to eliminating development charges on all residential developments from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029, reducing the cost of building new homes by up to $100,442 per home.

The $572 million in funding — with the federal government cost-matching the provincial government — will go toward projects like the widening of Barton Street into a five-lane multi-modal road from Fruitland Road to Fifty Road, widening Rymal Road, widening Garner Road, expanding the Woodward water and wastewater treatment plant, and upgrading the capacity of the Greenhill Water Pumping Station.

A few more announcements were made in September, but the pace of announcements hit another gear this month, with agreements with 11 municipalities announced. To date, agreements announced include:

  1. Hamilton: $572 million
  2. Vaughan: $697.2 million
  3. Bradford West Gwillimbury: $94.8 million
  4. Mississauga: $404.1 million
  5. Barrie: $129.2 million
  6. St. Thomas: $19.6 million
  7. Orillia: $11.3 million
  8. Guelph: $48.3 million
  9. Sudbury: $45.3 million
  10. Essex County: $51.2 million
  11. LaSalle: $25.4 million
  12. Essex Town: $8.8 million
  13. Lakeshore: $11.8 million
  14. Kingsville: $8.4 million
  15. Windsor: $77.6 million
  16. Tecumseh: $6.8 million.

In total, the announcements amount to $2.2 billion in infrastructure funding. In most cases, the agreements will see the local government reduce development charges by 30% to 100% from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029.

One announcement that was slightly different was that for Mississauga, whose agreement runs from January 29, 2025 to March 31, 2029, reflecting the fact that Mississauga had previously implemented a development charge incentive program on its own, prior to the Canada-Ontario agreement.

Another announcement that was a bit more unique was that for the County of Essex, whose agreement runs from March 30, 2026 to December 31, 2030. According to the announcement, Essex County is reducing development charges on a staggered timeline. The reduction will be 100% for 2026 and 2027, 75% for 2028, 50% in 2029, and 25% in 2030.

The range of infrastructure projects the $2.2 billion in funding will go towards include road, bus, water, and wastewater infrastructure projects that are described as “housing-enabling.”

Ontario is also home to municipalities that do not levy development charges, however, and the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario agreement recognizes that as well. In mid-August, the two governments announced a Non-Development Charge Municipalities Stream (Non-DC Stream) that will allow those governments to also receive infrastructure funding that will enable new housing development.

“Municipalities that do not levy development charges often face challenges funding infrastructure projects because they do not have access to this revenue tool,” said the two governments in the announcement. “At the same time, these municipalities face high construction costs, aging assets and significant infrastructure backlogs.”

The Development Cost Reduction Program began accepting applications under the Non-DC Stream on October 29, 2026, with additional intakes expected to be announced at a later date.

The Development Cost Reduction Program is, of course, just one half of the Canada-Ontario deal, with the other being the 13% HST rebate from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027. The HST relief has sparked market activity in certain areas and segments of the market, although the market has still been fairly subdued.

The HST has also been the envy of the real estate industry in British Columbia, which has continued to push for similar relief. The Governments of Canada and British Columbia reached a deal in June that was similar to the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario deal, but it did not include the tax relief component. The deal did include development charge relief, but the program and agreements were not finalized prior to the snap election held earlier this month.

items.title: Canada’s GDP stalls, clouding Bank of Canada’s December call
items.description: Weak August data and a likely September contraction test the Bank of Canada’s resolve on rates
items.content: <p>Weak August data and a likely September contraction test the Bank of Canada’s resolve on rates</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639289647421852556.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Weak August data and a likely September contraction test the Bank of Canada’s resolve on rates
items.body:
Canada’s economy failed to grow for a second consecutive month in August, and Statistics Canada’s advance estimate for September points to a 0.1% contraction. The outcome lands below the Bank of Canada’s own projections just 48 hours after the central bank’s first rate hike since 2023.

Statistics Canada reported Friday that real gross domestic product was essentially unchanged in August. A 1.4% drop in wholesale trade and a 0.2% fall in the public sector aggregate, its first decline in six months, outweighed gains in retail trade, manufacturing, and construction.

Should the advance September estimate hold, third-quarter annualised growth would reach only 1.3%, against the Bank of Canada’s own 2% forecast.

The Bank raised its overnight rate to 2.50% on October 28, framing the move as risk management against energy-driven inflation. Friday’s GDP data offers a pointed counterpoint.

Benjamin Reitzes of BMO says the Bank of Canada's first rate hike in more than three years may not be its last, with future decisions likely hinging on economic growth, inflation trends, and incoming data over the months ahead. https://t.co/lcW0HncB9d — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 29, 2026

Retail and manufacturing hold the line

Retail trade gained 1.2% in August after contracting in July. Manufacturing rose 0.3%, its fifth increase in seven months, despite continued exposure to US tariffs. Construction added 0.2%.

Against those gains, utilities fell 0.4%, led by a 0.5% decline in electric power generation.

Public administration retreated as 2026 census preparation wound down. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction were flat.

What the shortfall means for December

Money markets are currently pricing in a hold at the Bank of Canada’s December 10 meeting, followed by a further 25-basis-point increase to 2.75% in January. Friday’s figures complicate that picture.

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics, said the report missed in more than one direction.

“This was a disappointing report relative to expectations and, more importantly, Statistics Canada’s guidance for September looks no better,” he said.

“Taken together, that leaves real GDP growth in the third quarter tracking around 1.3% annualized — still positive, but notably below the Bank of Canada’s recent projection.”

For mortgage brokers monitoring what the BoC’s next decision means for the mortgage market and advising clients through an increasingly complex renewal environment, the gap between growth momentum and Bank projections has become a defining tension heading into year-end.

That concern sits alongside the broader unease felt across the industry since Canada’s rate hike deepened broker worry over a struggling housing market.

Ercolao went further on the Bank’s 2027 outlook.

“For the Bank of Canada, today’s report may cast a little more doubt around the durability of the recovery heading into 2027,” he said.

“The Bank’s latest outlook anticipates a meaningful strengthening in growth next year, but signs of softer momentum heading into Q4 raise the bar for that forecast, particularly with trade uncertainty and higher energy costs still clouding the outlook. While the Bank remains focused on upside inflation risks following this week’s rate hike, weaker underlying growth could complicate the case for further tightening in the near-term.”

The pattern echoes the two straight quarters of GDP contraction in the first half of 2026 that had brokers watching the Bank’s every move, and the second half of the year has yet to deliver the rebound either the Bank or the broker community had anticipated.

items.title: One Way to Make Toronto Condos More Livable: Let Buyers Make Them Bigger
items.description:
For years, Toronto developers built condos that were an easy sell to investors, even if they weren’t ideal places to live. But with the market reckoning with a glut of “shoebox” inventory, the shortcomings of that approach are tough to ignore. Purchasers want more space from their condos; they want room to actually live.

That’s been a takeaway from One Ten Avenue Road, a boutique condominium coming up at the southern edge of Midtown Toronto, where Yorkville meets The Annex. The building will be 12 storeys with just 72 private suites, and according to Managing Partner at Sierra Building Group Jeffrey Kansun, around 45% of purchasers have chosen to merge multiple units.

This is a central feature of Sierra’s “Crafted by You” program. It’s not unusual for pre-con buyers to be able to pick their finishings and fixtures, but at One Ten Ave. purchasers are also getting a say in size and layout.

Richard Wengle Architect Inc.

“It’s been a response to the market from day one. Not everyone’s wishes fit into a box, literally and figuratively,” says Kansun. “We developed this program in response to customers — we didn’t have this idea when we started this project.”

In the first six months of presales, Sierra didn’t sell a single unit smaller than 2,500 square feet. The buyers, Kansun says, tend to be later-career homeowners who want to trade the responsibilities of a large house for something more manageable — without sacrificing so much of the space they’re used to.

That said, the need for more space is something that transcends any one type of condo buyer. A recent analysis by proptech platform Wahi found that three- and four-plus-bedroom units have held their value much better than their smaller counterparts — even with sales down across all the board. While the median sale price of a one-bedroom condo in the GTA fell 14% between the first quarter of 2020 and the first quarter of 2026 (to $480,000), two-beds rose 2% (to $630,000), three-beds rose 13% (to $700,000), and four-plus-beds rose 15% (to $715,000).

“In today’s GTA condo market, the end user is the main source of anything resembling demand,” Wahi Economist Ryan McLaughlin said in the report. “There simply isn’t much appetite among buyers for smaller units, which have historically been geared primarily towards investors looking to flip them or rent them out.”

For Richard Wengle, founder of Richard Wengle Architect Inc. and the principal architect for One Ten Ave., designing for the end user has long been central to his work. Wengle’s firm has been working on projects that allow for this kind of customization since around 2011, starting with The Randall in Oakville. Since then, the firm has worked with purchasers at One Forest Hill and 89 Avenue Road (among others) to tailor layouts to their needs, including combining units to create larger, more personalized homes.

For One Ten Ave., the “typical wish-list” for units that are being combined includes things like a large kitchen and dining room, generous closet space and extra storage, and a larger patio space than you would see attached to a Toronto-area condo. These are the kinds of features that purchasers — Wengle calls them “right-sizers” — are usually giving up when moving from a home to a condo.

And then there are other requests that require a more inventive architectural approach. “One purchaser is taking one floor and part of the floor below, where they'll have a separate private section that might be for kids that come to visit,” says Wengle. “So they're not necessarily walking through space that's not being used all the time and feeling like it's wasted.”

Of course, there are limits to the program. Plumbing and mechanical stacks, elevators, corridors, and structural elements are fixed, but non-load-bearing walls can often be moved to create a layout that better suits the owner. The goal is to work within those constraints while making the most of a unit’s views, natural light, and access to outdoor space.

For now, this kind of customization remains easier to offer in the luxury market, where buyers have the budgets to purchase additional square footage and manage the costs of the architectural services and — because customized layouts require more oversight and coordination to execute — higher construction management costs for the developer. But Kansun hopes the principle behind the approach is something that will catch on in the broader pre-con condo market.

“A lot of developers stuck with very small, un-livable units, and the values have just plummeted because of it. And the unfortunate reality is that it makes sense — you can’t really sell a unit that you can’t live in,” he says. “We, as an industry, will hopefully not make the same mistake twice.”

items._ogDesc: The CMHC forecasts Canadian mortgage arrears will hit a 9-year high by 2027. Here is why the national housing agency might be underestimating the fallout.
items.body:
Canada’s national housing agency is bearish on real estate over the near term. The CMHC’s latest forecast shows Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) mortgage arrears climbing into 2027. The trend is driven almost entirely by a surge in Ontario. That suggests they might be underestimating the fallout, since home prices in other provinces are only just starting to correct.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Have Climbed Aggressively

The arrears rate at Canada’s banks is on an aggressive climb. The share of mortgages in arrears hit 0.29% in July, up 6 basis points (bps) from last year. That’s the highest rate since 2015, more than doubling from the record low less than 5 years ago. It isn’t over either.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Forecast To Keep Climbing

Canadian mortgage arrears rate (90 days past due) and CMHC forecast.

Source: CBA; CMHC; Better Dwelling.

The CMHC forecasts the arrears rate will continue to rise through mid-2027. They expect it to hit 0.33% by February and hold there through June 2027, the end of the forecast period. That would push arrears to the highest level since 2012.

Why The CMHC Might Be Underestimating Arrears

A closer look at the forecast reveals the agency might be underestimating the stress. The projection is primarily driven by a 58% surge in arrears in Ontario, one of 2 provinces ending the forecast at a cycle high. Slow real estate sales, a rocky job market, and a price correction are cited as the drivers. However, they’re missing a key detail—other provinces haven’t seen a correction yet.

Canadian home prices made a substantial correction after most markets slipped in 2022. However, Ontario and BC are the only provinces to see a major correction, and only the former’s drop is bigger than the national average. Despite prices across the country getting a massive lift from the low-rate boom, all but 2 remain just off record highs. Slow sales are lingering as a result of market inefficiencies that still need to correct.

These provinces don’t appear to be immune to gravity, though. Last month, prices in regions that largely resisted the correction began making near-record declines. The declines have only just started in most of the country, potentially spreading Ontario’s climate to more markets. That would prove to be a major headwind for arrears in those regions.

items.title: B.C. investors turn to retail plazas amid tight supply: report
items.description: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items._ogDesc: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items.body:
Neighbourhood retail vacancy has fallen below one per cent in some Metro Vancouver suburbs as investors turn to established properties, according to a new report.

The Re/Max Canada Fall 2026 Commercial Real Estate Report, released Thursday, found that retail vacancy had fallen below three per cent in downtown Vancouver and less than one per cent in some suburban neighbourhoods.

Conditions across B.C. remain uneven as some other markets, including Kelowna, has been more subdued with limited new building supply weighing on rental conditions and higher costs slowing development, the report said.

“Supply has become increasingly constrained in some of the country’s key commercial markets,” said Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada.

Commercial real estate investors in B.C. are favouring neighbourhood retail plazas and existing industrial properties, as demand for well-located space remains strong. Meanwhile, high construction and financing costs are weighing on new development, according to the report.

“We've seen considerable investment in established, income-producing properties this year, particularly in markets where demand remains strong,” said Kristie Kimnach, executive director of Re/Max Commercial, in a statement.

“The challenge in some of these markets seems to have been finding enough quality products to meet investor demand.”

Neighbourhood shopping plazas and grocery-anchored centres have attracted tenants in sectors including medical services, health, wellness, beauty and food services, the report said.

However, strong demand for industrial space has not necessarily translated into higher sale prices in Greater Vancouver. Industrial sale prices softened even as availability tightened, according to the report.

Kottick said the imbalance between strong demand for established retail space—particularly smaller units in high-demand markets—and a lack of new developments could persist amid higher bond yields and economic uncertainty.

Nationally, 11 of the 12 markets examined reported improving industrial market conditions, measured by increasing absorption and decreasing availability. Retail conditions improved in 10 markets, while multi-family improved in seven markets.

Looking ahead to 2027, Re/Max anticipates a gradual and uneven recovery in Canada's commercial real estate market.

“While demand for established, income-producing properties is expected to remain strong, limited new construction could create further supply challenges in markets where demand continues to grow,” the report said.

The report draws on data and insights from Re/Max brokers and agents across 12 major Canadian markets, comparing activity from January to June 2026 with the same period a year earlier.
